metadata.note: The Montpelier & Wells River Railroad, the line that ran east out of Vermont's capital across the spine of the state to the Connecticut River, and its Barre branch into the granite city. Added because the dataset had Montpelier covered from the west (the Vermont Central branch in vermont_central_railroad.geojson, and today's Vermonter in amtrak.geojson and montrealer.geojson) but nothing at all going east: Wells River had no line within 15 km and Barre - the largest town in central Vermont - sat 8 km from the nearest track. Locals called it the Milk Run: it stopped in every village, carried passengers, mail, milk and lumber, and ran for 83 years. Geometry is real right-of-way from OpenStreetMap, identified by the old_railway_operator=B&M tagging on the abandoned roadbed. The two features differ sharply in quality and should be read differently: the Barre branch is still active Washington County Railroad track and is traced almost continuously (six bridged gaps, none over 365 m), while the main line east of Montpelier was pulled up in 1957 and survives in OSM only as disconnected fragments of roadbed - about 40 percent of that line's 37 miles is straight-line interpolation across unmapped gaps, none longer than 1 km. It follows the true corridor within a few hundred metres but is not a continuous survey. Era boundaries follow real, sourced corporate milestones; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not real timetables.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Montpelier_and_Wells_River_Railroad (chartered November 6 1867 under Vermont special legislation; construction begun about November 1 1870; opened for operation in two sections September 15 and November 24 1873; reincorporated January 1 1877 by court decree after financial difficulty, the property then being Montpelier to Wells River 38.22 miles plus Montpelier to Barre Transfer 1.79 miles; the Barre Branch Railroad incorporated June 15 1888 and opened June 1 1889, 3.38 miles Montpelier to Barre, leased to the parent at $4,800 a year and merged into the Montpelier and Wells River September 18 1913; a 1.67-mile section inside Barre leased from the Barre and Chelsea Railroad at $1,000 a year)

https://www.crossvermont.org/our_trail/trackthebed.php (Cross Vermont Trail Association, which owns and interprets much of the roadbed: trains ran 83 years, 1873 to 1956, stopping in every village with passengers, mail, milk and lumber - the Milk Run; the Montpelier depot stood at Taylor Street where the Shaws grocery is now, with shops along today's Stonecutters Way; the Barre spur split off at Barre Transfer near the present Route 2/Route 302 roundabout; stations at Fairmont in East Montpelier, Plainfield village, Marshfield village, Lanesboro and Groton village through Groton State Forest, South Ryegate and Boltonville; four tracks met in a wye at Wells River; last train November 15 1956, rails removed March 1957)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Barre_and_Chelsea_Railroad (Barre Railroad Company incorporated April 9 1888, merged with the East Barre and Chelsea Railroad Company in 1913 to become the Barre and Chelsea; 13.819 miles of main track from Barre to the granite quarries and East Barre; controlled by the Vermont Valley Railroad, a lessor of the Boston and Maine; owned but leased 1.673 miles to the Montpelier and Wells River for $1,000 a year; under United States Railroad Administration control from 1918 until February 1920)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montpelier_station_(Vermont) (the Vermont Central built its branch to downtown Montpelier in 1849 and regular service on that branch was discontinued in 1938, replaced by a bus - context for why the capital's rail service shifted to Montpelier Junction)

https://plainfieldvthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/VermontTrains-PartII.pdf (Plainfield Historical Society, 'Vermont Trains Part II': opening service 1873, '1945 re-organized as the Barre & Chelsea', dated photographs of mixed trains with combine No. 14 to November 1956, last run November 15 1956)
https://www.branchline.uk/jfpdf/vermontrrs.pdf (John Fowler, Vermont Railroads Passenger Stations & Stops, sections 25-26: letters s = 1891 timetable, c = 1935 M&WR timetable, d = 1953 B&C timetable)
https://nashuacitystation.org/history/barre-and-chelsea-railroad-company/ (Barre and Chelsea acquired the Montpelier and Wells River December 1944)

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Frequency for every era is estimated. Montpelier - Barre: passenger service is confirmed only 1891-1935 [OPEN]; it ended at an unknown year between 1935 and September 1951 (freight only in the February 1952 Official Guide), and the 1889-1890 years after opening have no passenger listing. Main line: the exact day of the M&WR -> Barre and Chelsea change (December 1944 vs 1945) is not pinned down, and whether the Boston & Maine actually ran the trains 1911-1926 (Plainfield Historical Society) or only controlled the company (Barre Daily Times 1912) is unresolved - the ICC M&WR valuation text is the place to check for an operating agreement. The measured Montpelier-Barre branch runs 6.5 miles against the 1.79 + 3.38 miles the ICC valuation gives for its two pieces; the difference is yard and terminal trackage at both ends of the modern active line.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.barre_and_chelsea_audit: 2026-10-15, from research/branches/barre_and_chelsea_railroad.txt: (1) Rule 4 ownership split - montpelier-wells-river-main's last segment cut from 1913-1956 to 1913-1945; the Barre and Chelsea's operation of the same track 1945-1956 is now its own feature on identical geometry, bc-montpelier-wells-river in barre_and_chelsea_railroad.geojson. (2) montpelier-barre-branch cut from 1889-1956 to 1891-1935 [OPEN]: start moved from the 1889 opening to the first passenger timetable (1891), end from the 1956 abandonment of the main line to the last confirmed passenger timetable (1935) - the September 1951 Official Guide shows the branch freight only (Rule 1). (3) montpelier-barre-branch recoloured from #8C5E58 to the M&WR's #3F7D20 and its company changed from 'Barre Branch Railroad (Montpelier and Wells River Railroad)' to 'Montpelier and Wells River Railroad' (Rule 4): the Barre Branch Railroad was a paper lessor and the M&WR ran the trains throughout. Segment notes and sources rewritten for the changed segments. (4) geometry_quality strings added to both features (they had none), restating the layer metadata's own account of the trace.

segments.note: The Barre Branch was merged into the Montpelier & Wells River on September 18 1913. Locals knew the line as the Milk Run: it stopped in every village along the way, carrying passengers, mail, milk and lumber; passengers were photographed boarding at Groton in July 1942 (Plainfield Historical Society). This feature ends at the Montpelier & Wells River's sale to the Barre and Chelsea Railroad - December 1944 per Nashua City Station (citing Lindsell 2000 and the ICC), '1945 re-organized as the Barre & Chelsea' per the Plainfield Historical Society; the exact day the Barre and Chelsea name went onto the trains is not established. 1945 is shared with the Barre and Chelsea feature (barre_and_chelsea_railroad.geojson, id bc-montpelier-wells-river), which draws the same track 1945-1956, following the repo's boundary-year convention for ownership splits. Unresolved: the Plainfield Historical Society says the line 'became operated by the Boston & Maine' 1911-1926; the Barre Daily Times (1912) shows B&M control through a common president with trains and new coaches still in the M&WR's name, so no B&M split is drawn. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: the 1945 end (ownership change to the Barre and Chelsea) is from Nashua City Station and the Plainfield Historical Society; the 1913 start is the ICC valuation's merger date. Headway is an estimate, not sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Drawn 37.0 mi against 37.9 mi documented Montpelier - Wells River (Official Guide Sept 1951 and Fowler agree; the ICC valuation gives 38.22 mi) - 2% short. The line was lifted in 1957 and survives in OSM only as disconnected roadbed fragments tagged old_railway_operator=B&M; per this layer's metadata about 40 percent of the 37 miles is straight-line interpolation across unmapped gaps. Those approximated legs were not named individually when the layer was built and have not been re-derived (the longest single vertex-to-vertex leg is 2.3 km, so the metadata's 'none longer than 1 km' is unverified). Ends at Wells River; the ~0.5 mi into Woodsville, NH over the Boston & Maine is not drawn. Geometry is shared, identically, with bc-montpelier-wells-river in barre_and_chelsea_railroad.geojson.

properties.line: Montpelier and Wells River: Montpelier – Barre
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Incorporated June 15 1888 and opened June 1 1889, the Barre Branch Railroad ran 3.38 miles from the Montpelier & Wells River main line at Barre Transfer into Barre, and was leased straight back to its parent for $4,800 a year; the M&WR ran the trains from the start, so the branch carries the M&WR's company and colour. The last 1.67 miles inside Barre, from Tilden Bridge to Ayer Street, were leased from the Barre Railroad (later Barre and Chelsea) from June 30 1894. Drawn from 1891, not the 1889 opening: an opening date is not a passenger date, and the first dated passenger listing found is the 1891 timetable in John Fowler's Vermont station list (Barre Transfer - Dodge Bridge - Sortwell & Morse Mills - North Barre - Silver Street - Barre, 'with sub[urban]' service). The Concord & Montreal's July 14 1894 guide also lists Barre on the M&WR route (Nashua City Station). An 1889 or 1890 timetable would restore the first two years. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: the 1891 start is Fowler's 1891 timetable letter (sections 25-26); the 1889 opening and 1913 merger are from the ICC valuation. Headway is an estimate, not sourced.

segments.note: Merged into the Montpelier & Wells River on September 18 1913. This was the granite branch: the Barre Railroad's quarry lines fed stone onto it, and it carried that and the town's passengers down to Montpelier. Passenger service confirmed to 1935 by the 1935 Montpelier & Wells River timetable (Fowler, letter c on Barre and Barre Transfer). This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when passenger service actually stopped. The September 30 1951 Barre and Chelsea table in the February 1952 Official Guide prints the Barre - Montpelier block as 'Freight Service only' (OCR '...vice only'), so passengers ended at an unknown year between 1935 and 1951; 1951-1956 is freight only and is not drawn. Do not extend without evidence. Freight continued: the Washington County Railroad still runs Montpelier - Barre freight today. A 2019 vermontbiz.com claim that the corridor saw no passenger rail after the trolley's 1927 demise is contradicted by the 1935 timetable listing and is recorded, not believed. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: the 1935 end is the last confirmed timetable listing (Fowler, letter c = 1935 M&WR timetable); the February 1952 Official Guide shows the branch freight only in September 1951. The 1913 start is the ICC valuation's merger date. Headway is an estimate, not sourced.

The Official Guide of the Railways, February 1952: Barre and Chelsea Railroad Company table dated September 30 1951 (Montpelier - Wells River - Woodsville with times; Barre - Montpelier block 'Freight Service only'); index of stations daggers Websterville freight only

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM on the active Washington County Railroad track (old_railway_operator=B&M), almost continuous: per this layer's metadata six gaps were bridged, none over 365 m. Drawn 6.5 mi Montpelier - Barre against 1.79 + 3.38 = 5.17 mi in the ICC valuation and Fowler's 4.5 mi (Barre Transfer at 1.9, Barre at 4.5) - 25-45% long, the excess being yard and terminal trackage of the modern line at both ends; the shared Montpelier - Barre Transfer stretch duplicates the main line. Drawn on the surviving modern alignment; whether it differs from the 1891-1935 passenger alignment has not been checked.
